extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and litigants involved in PTAB inter partes review (IPR) proceedings (petitioners, patent owners, and their counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria used by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) to evaluate patentability challenges in inter partes review, including real-party-in-interest rules, anticipation and obviousness analyses, claim construction, priority/written-description, and incorporation-by-reference issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-party-in-interest (RPI) naming is not jurisdictional (SharkNinja)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to name an RPI is “not jurisdictional” and an unnamed RPI can be added later (citing SharkNinja Operating LLC v. iRobot Corp.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although SharkNinja treats failure to name an RPI as non-jurisdictional, petitioners still bear the burden of demonstrating compliance with statutory requirements (e.g., 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(2) and § 315(b)). Evidence that an unnamed party is funding the petition, advising on strategy, or controlling decisions/arguments can bear on RPI/privity determinations. Mere co-ownership or the existence of a license does not alone make an entity a real party-in-interest or show privity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden to demonstrate compliance with 35 U.S.C. §312(a)(2) and §315(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners bear the burden of demonstrating compliance with 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(2) and § 315(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record must provide sufficient reason to doubt any assertion (for example, the petitioner's assertion that no unnamed party is funding, advising, or controlling the petition). If the record does not show such involvement, the petitioner’s assertions stand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation standard (35 U.S.C. §102)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated if “each and every limitation is found either expressly or inherently in a single prior art reference.” (Sanofi–Synthelabo v. Apotex).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation may be established by showing that all elements arranged as specified in a claim are disclosed within the four corners of a reference, either expressly or inherently, in a manner enabling a POSITA to practice an embodiment without undue experimentation (ClearValue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness standard (35 U.S.C. §103 and KSR/Graham framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable under §103(a) if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Graham factual inquiries: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claims and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness when in evidence. KSR v. Teleflex governs the legal standard; underlying factual determinations drive the obviousness conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the level of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various factors may be considered to determine the level of ordinary skill, including: type of problems encountered; prior art solutions; rapidity of innovations; sophistication of the technology; and educational level of active workers in the field (In re GPAC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A higher level of ordinary skill generally favors obviousness; a lower level generally favors nonobviousness. The Board may adopt a party's proposed POSITA if it is reasonable and consistent with the patent specification and prior art (Okajima v. Bourdeau). Example: petitioner proposed a POSITA with at least a bachelor’s in chemical/mechanical engineering and two years' experience, which the Board found reasonable on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (Phillips/district-court-type; 37 C.F.R. §42.100(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: In IPRs, claim language is interpreted using the district-court-type standard (Phillips): claim terms get their ordinary and customary meaning to a POSITA at the time of invention, in light of claim language, specification, and prosecution history; extrinsic evidence may be useful but is considered in context of intrinsic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board construes only those claim terms that are in controversy and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (Realtime Data v. Iancu). If no disputed construction is needed to resolve the grounds at the preliminary stage, the Board may decline explicit construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority-date and chain-of-applications requirement for priority
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim an earlier priority date from parent applications (including provisionals and continuations), the patent must demonstrate entitlement via the priority chain and written description support in the parent/priority applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If entitled to an earlier priority date, asserted prior art filed after that date may not qualify as prior art. The Board analyzes the chain (provisional → pre-CIP → post-CIP → later applications) and evaluates whether new limitations were present in earlier filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement for priority (cannot be satisfied by obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A priority application must itself describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail; entitlement does not extend to subject matter that would only be obvious over what is expressly disclosed (Ariad/Lockwood/PowerOasis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written description requires more than showing the claimed subject matter would have been obvious; the earlier application must actually describe the invention such that it 'particularly point[s] out and distinctly claim[s]' it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference specificity (Callaway Golf standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: To incorporate another document by reference, the host document must identify with detailed particularity what specific material it incorporates and clearly indicate where that material is found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous incorporation language (e.g., 'incorporated . . . to the extent appropriate') can raise issues of sufficiency and may be reserved for resolution at trial. The Board recognized potential ambiguity in phrasing that does not clearly identify what portion is incorporated.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §1.57(d) — essential material cannot be incorporated from a provisional
rubrics_metrics.description: Material that is 'essential' (necessary to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention, per 37 C.F.R. §1.57(d)(2)) may be incorporated by reference only via a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication; a U.S. provisional application is not a qualifying source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject matter relied upon for written description is 'essential' and was omitted from parent applications, incorporation by reference to a provisional is ineffective under §1.57(d). Thus omitted essential material disclosed only in a provisional generally cannot be used to support priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §1.57(b) — remedy for inadvertently omitted material and timing limits
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. §1.57(b) provides a procedure to consider omitted material from a priority application as incorporated by reference, but requires that the application be amended to include the omitted portion no later than the close of prosecution (or abandonment), among other requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An amendment adding omitted material after the close of prosecution is ineffective to restore the omitted subject matter; timing and procedural compliance are essential for §1.57(b) relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting specification examples and figures conservatively when assessing written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of exemplary injection points or examples in a specification (e.g., 'before, after, or within the boiler') may not support broader claim scope such as adding promoter to coal vs. adding to flue gas — the Board examines what the examples actually disclose rather than inferring broader coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A passage describing injection of a 'promoted sorbent' at multiple points does not necessarily disclose separate steps of (1) adding a promoter to coal/combustion chamber and (2) separately injecting sorbent downstream. The Board will compare the exact wording, figures, and context and will not accept mere obvious variations as satisfying written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation/enablement nexus — four-corners disclosure must enable practice
rubrics_metrics.description: For anticipation, the single reference must disclose all claim limitations within its four corners and in a way that enables a POSITA to practice an embodiment of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if every limitation appears to be described, the disclosure must be enabling; mere theoretical or model descriptions that do not show how to practice the claimed invention may be insufficient for anticipation.
